case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Congress may, consistent with the First Amendment and other constitutional limits, require TikTok/ByteDance to divest TikTok’s U.S. operations (or face an effective ban) based on national-security concerns tied to foreign-adversary control, and whether the Supreme Court should enjoin that requirement pending further review.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Protecting Americans From Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act (Div. H of Pub. L. 118-50, Apr. 24, 2024) and the U.S. Constitution—primarily the First Amendment (free speech), with some amici also invoking the Bill of Attainder Clause (Art. I, § 9, cl. 3).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: TikTok and ByteDance argue that the Act functions as a speech-restrictive ‘corporate death penalty’ targeted at a major communications platform and its users, triggering at least strict scrutiny under the First Amendment; they contend the forced divestiture/ban is not narrowly tailored and impermissibly burdens protected expression, and they seek an emergency injunction to prevent irreparable harm while Supreme Court review is pursued.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The government (and aligned amici such as Senator McConnell) argue the Act regulates nonexpressive conduct—foreign-adversary control and associated data-security/national-security risks—rather than suppressing any message or viewpoint, so it either does not implicate the First Amendment or easily survives heightened scrutiny; they further argue an injunction would undermine the public interest in national security and would effectively nullify Congress’s timetable by delaying enforcement into a new administration.
key_precedents: Arcara v. Cloud Books, Inc., 478 U.S. 697 (1986)
Police Department of Chicago v. Mosley, 408 U.S. 92 (1972)
Federal Election Commission v. International Funding Institute, Inc., 969 F.2d 1110 (D.C. Cir. 1992)
Moody v. NetChoice, LLC, 144 S. Ct. 2383 (2024)
United States v. Higgs, 141 S. Ct. 645 (2021) (mem)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s central point—that a platform-specific divest-or-cease regime predictably disables a major speech forum and thus may fall outside Arcara’s comfortable “incidental burden” category—deserves serious attention on the merits, and it cautions against overreading Arcara at this stage. But even accepting Justice Kagan’s observation (with Moody v. NetChoice in the background) that platforms can be expressive, the Act’s trigger remains foreign-adversary control with an off-ramp via divestiture, which on this emergency record keeps the measure structurally closer to an ownership/control regulation assessed under O’Brien/Ward than to Mosley-style content discrimination. The petitioners’ burden is a clear showing, and I do not see a sufficiently developed record demonstrating that Congress’s chosen divestiture mechanism burdens substantially more speech than necessary or that we should effectively extend Congress’s national-security timetable by injunction. A narrow denial of emergency relief—without prejudging the ultimate First Amendment standard or the availability of narrower remedies on a full record—best preserves institutional legitimacy while leaving the merits for orderly review.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is the Act’s platform-specific practical effect—disabling a major modern speech forum—which they argue takes this outside Arcara’s incidental-burden logic. But under a textualist/originalist approach, the statute’s operative trigger is not expressive activity or viewpoint; it is the status of being “foreign adversary controlled,” with a divestiture path that confirms Congress targeted control and attendant national-security risk rather than suppressing ideas, keeping the case closer to Arcara and O’Brien than Mosley. Justice Kagan’s invocation of Moody v. NetChoice usefully underscores that platforms can be speakers, yet it does not transform an ownership-and-control remedy into a content-based restriction when the law is keyed to control rather than speech. On this emergency record, petitioners have not made the clear showing required to enjoin an Act of Congress in an area touching foreign affairs, and I would not extend Congress’s timetable based on speculative less-restrictive alternatives not established here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that the Act’s platform-specific divest-or-cease structure predictably disables a major speech forum and thus may “inevitably” single out expressive activity under Arcara—warrants careful merits review, but it does not justify emergency injunctive relief on this record. The statute’s operative trigger is foreign-adversary ownership/control, and the divestiture option (as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize) demonstrates Congress targeted the control risk rather than suppressing any message, placing this closer to Arcara/O’Brien than Mosley even if the platform is “expressive” under Moody v. NetChoice. Justice Jackson’s less-restrictive-alternatives argument goes to tailoring, but at the injunction stage petitioners must make a clear showing; in a national-security and foreign-affairs setting, we should not effectively extend Congress’s timetable absent a far stronger record that the burden on speech is substantially greater than essential. Denying interim relief preserves our ability to decide the First Amendment questions on a full merits record without prematurely invalidating (or rewriting) an Act of Congress.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s institutional point about not deciding the merits on an emergency record is the strongest push, but it cuts both ways: if the record is too thin to uphold a platform-ending restriction, it is also too thin to allow a statute to take effect on a timetable that effectively moots meaningful First Amendment review for millions of speakers. I accept the respondents’ Arcara/O’Brien framing to a point—foreign-adversary control is not content-based—but Arcara’s comfort with “incidental” burdens weakens where (as here) the law is platform-specific and its predictable operation is to disable a speech forum rather than regulate generally applicable conduct, so some meaningful tailoring showing under O’Brien/Ward remains necessary. Justice Kavanaugh and others say petitioners have not clearly shown less restrictive alternatives, but on this posture it is the Government that has not persuasively explained why narrower data-security, governance, or mitigation measures cannot address the asserted risk without extinguishing the forum on the current schedule. Given that concrete, immediate, and irreparable loss of access will fall hardest on small creators and vulnerable speakers, the equities favor preserving the status quo pending full merits review rather than allowing a potentially unconstitutional speech burden to become fait accompli.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press that this Act is platform-specific and, as a practical matter, threatens a major speech forum—so Arcara’s “incidental burden” label cannot do all the work and we should not minimize the expressive impact. But on the statute’s text the trigger is “foreign adversary controlled” status with a divestiture path, which keeps the measure structurally in the lane of ownership/control regulation rather than Mosley-style content discrimination; that points to O’Brien/Ward intermediate scrutiny and, at this emergency stage, a heavy burden the petitioners have not clearly met on a thin record. Chief Justice Roberts’s institutional point about emergency relief is also decisive for me: enjoining enforcement would effectively reset Congress’s timetable in a national-security setting without the developed factual basis we normally demand before taking that step. Moody v. NetChoice, as several colleagues note, confirms platforms can be expressive, but it does not transform every control-and-security remedy into a content-based speech restriction, especially where divestiture preserves continued operation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson rightly press Arcara’s caveat about laws with the “inevitable effect” of singling out expressive venues, and I agree that the Act’s platform-specific operation warrants serious merits scrutiny. But under the statute’s text the operative trigger is “foreign adversary controlled” status and the remedy is divestiture as a condition of continued U.S. distribution—an ownership/control rule not keyed to any message, which keeps this closer to Arcara/O’Brien than Mosley’s content-discrimination framework even if the practical burden on speech is large. Justice Kagan’s reference to Moody v. NetChoice reinforces that recognizing platforms’ expressive interests does not transmute every structural, control-focused measure into content-based censorship; the question becomes whether the incidental burden is no greater than essential, and on this emergency record petitioners have not made the clear showing needed to halt an Act of Congress in an area touching foreign affairs. The equities argument for preserving the status quo cannot, in my view, substitute for that likelihood-of-success showing where Congress has provided a path for continued operation through divestiture.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best point: as a practical matter the Act risks disabling a major speech forum, and Arcara’s “incidental burden” label may be strained where a statute is platform-specific. But even taking that seriously, the statutory trigger remains foreign-adversary ownership/control with a divestiture path, which keeps the measure structurally closer to an ownership/control regulation than a Mosley-style content or viewpoint restriction, and thus more naturally analyzed under O’Brien/Ward on the present record. Chief Justice Roberts’s institutional/equitable concern is decisive for me at this stage: on an emergency application, petitioners must make a clear showing, and the Court should be cautious about effectively extending Congress’s timetable in an area touching national security without a full merits record. Sotomayor/Jackson’s less-restrictive-alternatives argument may have force on the merits, but it does not, on this emergency record, undermine the conclusion that petitioners have not clearly shown likely success or entitlement to extraordinary relief.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that a platform-specific divest-or-cease regime predictably disrupts a major modern speech forum, and Arcara cautions that we cannot ignore a law’s “inevitable effect” of singling out expressive activity. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief emphasize, the Act’s text triggers on “foreign adversary controlled” status and offers divestiture as an alternative, which is most naturally understood as an ownership/control rule aimed at a nonexpressive condition rather than a content- or viewpoint-based restraint under Mosley. Even recognizing, per Moody v. NetChoice, that platforms have expressive interests, that recognition does not itself convert a structural, control-focused remedy into censorship; at most it points to O’Brien/Ward intermediate scrutiny, and on this emergency record petitioners have not made the clear showing that Congress’s mechanism burdens substantially more speech than necessary relative to the asserted national-security/data-security interests. Given the extraordinary nature of emergency relief and the institutional concerns Chief Justice Roberts flags about effectively revising Congress’s timetable in a national-security setting, I would deny an injunction without prejudging the merits on a fuller record.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s emergency-posture point is the strongest counterweight: we should be wary of effectively extending Congress’s timetable in a national-security setting on a thin record. But Arcara’s “incidental burden” comfort (as Roberts, Justice Thomas, and Justice Alito invoke) depended on a generally applicable measure whose practical operation did not predictably shutter a central speech forum; here, the platform-specific divest-or-ban structure makes the expressive burden foreseeable and effectively unavoidable for millions during merits litigation, which heightens the procedural-fairness case for preserving the status quo. Justice Kagan’s O’Brien/Ward framing is plausible and Moody v. NetChoice underscores that platforms can have expressive dimensions, yet even under intermediate scrutiny the government must show the speech burden is no greater than essential—and on this emergency record the breadth and compressed timetable are not adequately justified relative to less speech-restrictive security alternatives. Because denial risks irreparable, widespread speech disruption that cannot be meaningfully remedied later, I would grant interim relief without prejudging the ultimate merits.

John Roberts.reasoning: At this preliminary stage, petitioners have not made the clear showing necessary for emergency injunctive relief, particularly given Congress’s express national-security judgment in the Protecting Americans From Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act and the strong public-interest weight traditionally afforded to foreign-affairs and security measures. The Act is best understood as regulating nonexpressive conduct—foreign-adversary control and associated data-security risks—rather than suppressing any viewpoint or message, bringing it within the conduct-versus-speech framework of Arcara v. Cloud Books, Inc., where incidental burdens on expressive activity did not trigger invalidation of an otherwise valid statute. Even assuming some First Amendment scrutiny applies, the statute’s structural focus on ownership/control (not content) and its divestiture option weigh against treating it as a content-based restriction under Mosley, and the Court should proceed narrowly without enjoining Congress’s chosen timetable. Respect for institutional legitimacy and the need to avoid effectively deciding the merits on an emergency record counsel denying an injunction while further review proceeds.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under a textualist and original-public-meaning approach, the First Amendment forbids laws “abridging the freedom of speech,” not Congress’s regulation of foreign-adversary control over a commercial entity’s U.S. operations pursuant to its national-security and foreign-affairs powers, as reflected in the Protecting Americans From Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act. The Act targets nonexpressive conduct—ownership/control by a foreign adversary and attendant data-security risks—and any burden on speech is incidental, placing this case within Arcara v. Cloud Books, Inc., 478 U.S. 697, 706–07 (1986), rather than Mosley’s content-based framework. Even assuming some First Amendment scrutiny applies, the statute is content- and viewpoint-neutral and would be evaluated under O’Brien-type intermediate scrutiny, where the Government’s national-security interest is weighty and the remedy (divestiture as an alternative to prohibition) is tailored to the control risk rather than to any message. Because petitioners have not shown a clear likelihood of success on the merits, the Court should not enjoin Congress’s chosen timetable pending further review.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Act regulates foreign-adversary control of a major communications platform as a matter of national security and data protection, not the content or viewpoint of any speech, and thus is best understood as regulation of nonexpressive conduct with at most incidental effects on expression. Under Arcara v. Cloud Books, Inc., 478 U.S. 697, 706-07 (1986), First Amendment scrutiny is not triggered where the law targets nonexpressive activity and does not inevitably single out expressive activity; even if some scrutiny applies, the divestiture requirement readily satisfies intermediate scrutiny under United States v. O’Brien because it advances an important governmental interest unrelated to suppressing expression. The statute is textually framed as a divest-or-cease-to-operate mechanism keyed to “foreign adversary controlled” status, not speech, and Congress’s foreign-affairs and national-security judgments warrant substantial deference when evaluating equities for emergency relief. Given the strong public interest in avoiding national-security harm and the Act’s content-neutral structure, the Court should deny an injunction pending further review.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Even accepting Congress’s national-security aims, this Act effectively conditions the continued operation of a major communications platform on government-approved ownership, imposing a sweeping burden on the speech and associational interests of millions of U.S. users and creators; that practical impact triggers meaningful First Amendment scrutiny rather than being treated as a merely incidental regulation of conduct. Arcara v. Cloud Books, Inc. allows regulation of nonexpressive conduct without heightened scrutiny only when it does not have the “inevitable effect of singling out those engaged in expressive activity,” but here Congress has identified and effectively shut down a specific, speech-intensive forum unless it divests—something far closer to targeted suppression than a general law. Even under intermediate scrutiny frameworks like O’Brien, the government must show the burden on expression is no greater than essential, and on this emergency posture the record does not yet justify why less speech-restrictive alternatives (e.g., tailored data-security mandates) are inadequate given the Act’s broad remedial sweep. Because the loss of an entire platform as a speech forum constitutes irreparable harm and the equities for vulnerable speakers and small creators run strongly toward preserving access while the merits are fully reviewed, I would enjoin enforcement pending further review.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Act’s operative trigger is not any message or viewpoint on TikTok, but “foreign adversary” control and the attendant national-security/data-security risks; under Arcara v. Cloud Books, a law aimed at nonexpressive conduct that does not have the “inevitable effect” of singling out expressive activity does not, on that basis alone, trigger the most searching First Amendment scrutiny. Even assuming some First Amendment burden on a communications platform and its users, the divestiture remedy functions as a content-neutral regulation of ownership/control and would be assessed under an O’Brien/Ward-style intermediate-scrutiny framework, where Congress’s national-security interest is substantial and the statute is structured to avoid suppressing speech by allowing continued operation upon divestiture (Protecting Americans From Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act, Div. H of Pub. L. 118-50). Given the heavy public interest in national security and the fact that an injunction would effectively extend Congress’s deadline and alter the statutory scheme pending review, the equitable factors cut against emergency relief. Moody v. NetChoice underscores that platforms can be engaged in protected expression, but it does not convert every structural/ownership regulation into content-based censorship, especially where the law’s aim is control and security rather than the suppression of ideas.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: On the Act’s plain terms, Congress has regulated ownership and control of a covered application by a “foreign adversary,” conditioning continued U.S. operation on divestiture rather than restricting any particular ideas, subjects, or viewpoints; that looks like regulation of nonexpressive conduct with only incidental effects on speech. Under Arcara v. Cloud Books, a law aimed at nonexpressive activity does not trigger the same First Amendment solicitude merely because it burdens an entity that also facilitates expression, and nothing in the statute turns on content as in Mosley. Even assuming intermediate scrutiny applies under O’Brien principles, Congress’s national-security and data-security interests are substantial and the divest-or-cease-operating mechanism is directed to foreign-adversary control rather than message suppression. Given the strong presumption against enjoining an Act of Congress and the equities the government asserts in national security, petitioners have not shown the clear likelihood of success and irreparable harm necessary for emergency injunctive relief pending further review.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Act primarily regulates nonexpressive conduct—foreign-adversary ownership/control of a major communications platform—rather than suppressing any particular message or viewpoint, and under Arcara v. Cloud Books it does not automatically trigger strict First Amendment scrutiny merely because compliance will have incidental effects on speech. Even assuming heightened scrutiny applies, the divestiture option makes the measure more akin to an ownership/structural regulation evaluated under O’Brien-style intermediate scrutiny, and Congress’s national-security and foreign-affairs judgments here are entitled to substantial respect as a practical matter. At the emergency-injunction stage, petitioners have not shown a clear likelihood of success or that the equities justify effectively suspending a congressionally chosen timetable in an area touching national security. An injunction pending further review would risk undermining the public interest and the Court’s institutional role by prematurely overriding Congress’s considered judgment without a full merits record.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: On the Act’s text, Congress regulates foreign-adversary control of a specific application by requiring divestiture as a condition of continued U.S. distribution, addressing ownership and data-security risk rather than suppressing any viewpoint or subject matter. Under Arcara v. Cloud Books, a law aimed at nonexpressive conduct does not trigger heightened First Amendment scrutiny merely because it incidentally burdens expressive activity, and this Act is best characterized as such a regulation of control/operations rather than speech. Even assuming First Amendment scrutiny applies, the statute is plausibly content-neutral and would be evaluated under O’Brien/Ward intermediate scrutiny; protecting national security and Americans’ data from a hostile foreign power is an important governmental interest, and divestiture is materially less speech-restrictive than a direct content-based ban. Given the heavy equitable burden for emergency injunctive relief and the public-interest weight in national security, I would not enjoin the divestiture requirement pending further review.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Act (Div. H of Pub. L. 118-50) is framed as regulating foreign-adversary control, but as applied it effectively disables a major communications platform and burdens the expressive activity of millions of U.S. users, raising serious First Amendment concerns under Mosley’s insistence on skepticism toward laws that selectively burden expressive channels. Arcara permits treating some closures as regulation of nonexpressive conduct only where the law neither targets expressive activity nor has the inevitable effect of singling out speakers; here, the statute’s platform-specific structure and practical consequences risk doing exactly that, at least enough to warrant heightened scrutiny rather than a deferential incidental-burden analysis. Even assuming intermediate scrutiny under O’Brien, the Government has not, on the current emergency record, shown that a forced divestiture-or-ban on this timetable is narrowly tailored to the national-security interest or that less speech-burdensome alternatives (e.g., concrete data-security and governance remedies) are inadequate. Given the severe, immediate, and potentially irreversible impact on public discourse, procedural fairness and the equities favor enjoining enforcement pending full merits review.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Congress may require TikTok/ByteDance to divest TikTok’s U.S. operations (or face an effective U.S. distribution/operation ban) on foreign-adversary national-security grounds without violating the First Amendment and other structural constitutional limits, and whether an emergency injunction pending Supreme Court review should issue.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Protecting Americans From Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act (Pub. L. 118-50, Div. H, Apr. 24, 2024) (the “Act”); U.S. Const. amend. I (speech); U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3 (Bill of Attainder Clause).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: TikTok and ByteDance seek an injunction pending Supreme Court review to prevent the statutory divestiture deadline from taking effect. Their core merits theory is that forcing divestiture (on pain of an app-store/hosting style prohibition) burdens protected expressive activity and thus violates the First Amendment, and that the statute is constitutionally suspect because it effectively singles out TikTok by name and targets it for severe legal consequences without the protections of ordinary adjudicatory process (including an argument, raised by amici, that the Act operates like a modern bill of attainder by legislatively identifying a disfavored entity and imposing punitive consequences). They also stress irreparable harm if divestiture occurs before final review.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States (and supporting amici like Senator McConnell) argue the Act is a national-security/data-security regulation directed at non-expressive conduct—foreign-adversary control and associated risks to Americans’ data—not at speech or viewpoint. Under that framing, the Act either does not trigger heightened First Amendment scrutiny at all, or at minimum survives even strict scrutiny because Congress acted to address compelling national-security interests through a tailored divestiture mechanism. On emergency relief, they argue delay is contrary to the public interest because an injunction would effectively extend the statutory divestiture deadline into a new administration, undermining Congress’s chosen timetable; they characterize TikTok’s emergency posture as a strategic attempt to run out the clock.
key_precedents: Arcara v. Cloud Books, Inc., 478 U.S. 697 (1986)
Police Dept. of Chicago v. Mosley, 408 U.S. 92 (1972)
FEC v. Int’l Funding Inst., Inc., 969 F.2d 1110 (D.C. Cir. 1992)
Moody v. NetChoice, LLC, 144 S. Ct. 2383 (2024)
United States v. Higgs, 141 S. Ct. 645 (2021) (mem)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that naming a specific platform and threatening its disappearance imposes a grave, immediate burden on a major speech forum, and Moody’s recognition that platform operations can be expressive sharpens that concern. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, the statute’s trigger is foreign-adversary “control” and the remedy is divestiture-or-disablement—a structural market-access condition that targets nonexpressive ownership attributes rather than any message, speaker, or viewpoint, which keeps Arcara relevant and at most moves us into O’Brien/Ward intermediate scrutiny. On this emergency record, petitioners have not made the required clear showing that Congress’s national-security rationale is a pretext for speech suppression or that less restrictive alternatives are so obvious as to render the chosen means likely unconstitutional. Given the institutional and equitable costs of freezing Congress’s timetable in a foreign-affairs/national-security setting without full merits briefing, I would deny emergency relief on narrow grounds without prejudging the ultimate First Amendment questions.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that naming a particular platform and threatening loss of distribution can substantially burden a modern speech forum, and Moody v. NetChoice confirms that platforms’ operational choices may carry expressive dimensions. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the Act’s text triggers on foreign-adversary “control” and supplies a structural divest-or-disable condition of market access; under Arcara, that is regulation of nonexpressive ownership and security risk, not censorship of messages or viewpoints, even if the downstream speech effects are significant. Moody does not convert every structural or national-security ownership restriction touching a communications medium into a content-based speech regulation like Mosley; at most it suggests O’Brien/Ward intermediate scrutiny, and on this emergency record petitioners have not made the clear, strong showing needed to justify halting Congress’s foreign-affairs timetable. The bill-of-attainder theory remains weak under Nixon because the statute operates prospectively and conditionally, keyed to control attributes rather than legislative punishment for past conduct.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to stress that naming a particular platform and risking its disappearance burdens a major speech forum and is not "incidental" in the colloquial sense; in light of Moody v. NetChoice, we should not pretend platform operation is speech-free. But Arcara still frames the key inquiry as what the statute regulates on its face: here the trigger is foreign-adversary “control” and the remedy is divest-or-disable, a structural condition aimed at ownership-linked security risks rather than suppressing any message, speaker, or viewpoint. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, even if we move to O’Brien/Ward intermediate scrutiny, petitioners have not made the clear emergency-posture showing that Congress’s national-security rationale is pretextual or that an injunction is warranted to upend Congress’s timetable on a thin record. The bill-of-attainder theory likewise remains weak under Nixon’s functional framework because the Act is prospective and conditional rather than punitive for past conduct.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan press Arcara and the emergency-posture point—that the Act targets foreign-adversary “control” and any speech burden is incidental—but that framing understates how the statute operates: it singles out a specific, dominant speech forum by name and makes continued hosting/distribution unlawful unless a compelled ownership change occurs, a mechanism that predictably shuts down a channel for millions of lawful speakers. Justice Kagan is right that, at most, this pushes us into O’Brien/Ward; but under that framework the government still must show the chosen means are no more speech-restrictive than necessary, and on this record the divest-or-disable remedy looks blunt compared to narrower data-security/CFIUS-style tools that do not extinguish an existing forum while merits review proceeds. Justice Kavanaugh’s timetable/national-security equity argument is weighty, yet irreparable loss of lawful speech and association during the interim is also a public-interest harm, especially for vulnerable communities who disproportionately rely on low-barrier platforms for expression and organizing. Nixon/Arcara may ultimately defeat the bill-of-attainder theory, but the Act’s platform-specific design reinforces the need for caution before allowing an effective nationwide shutdown without fuller merits development.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press that naming a particular platform and threatening an effective shutdown makes the speech burden concrete rather than “fortuitous,” so Arcara cannot be used as a categorical off-switch for First Amendment scrutiny. But I still think the better textual and structural account—echoed by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh—is that the Act’s trigger is foreign-adversary “control” and the remedy is divest-or-disable, which regulates a nonexpressive ownership condition rather than any message, speaker, or viewpoint, placing us (at most) in O’Brien/Ward territory rather than strict scrutiny or Mosley-style analysis. Moody’s recognition that platform curation can be expressive matters, yet it does not convert every structural ownership or national-security condition on a communications business into content-based censorship; it simply means we should acknowledge incidental speech effects and ask whether Congress chose a reasonably tailored, workable means given its foreign-affairs/data-security interest. On this emergency posture, I agree with Roberts that petitioners have not made the clear, strong showing of likely success (including obvious less-restrictive alternatives on this record) necessary to justify enjoining Congress’s timetable in a national-security setting.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to stress that a named-platform statute with an effective “divest-or-disappear” consequence can impose profound, irreparable burdens on a major speech forum, and that fact counsels caution on the merits. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the Act’s text triggers on foreign-adversary “control” and supplies a structural remedy (divestiture as a condition of U.S. distribution/hosting), which—under Arcara—looks like regulation of nonexpressive ownership/control attributes rather than suppression of any message or viewpoint. Moody v. NetChoice, which Justice Kagan invokes, reinforces that platforms can engage in protected expression, yet it does not transform every ownership or national-security restriction affecting a communications medium into content-based censorship; at most it situates us in O’Brien/Ward-style intermediate scrutiny where Congress’s foreign-affairs and security interests are substantial. On this emergency posture, I do not see petitioners making the clear showing required to enjoin Congress’s timetable absent stronger evidence that the law’s inevitable effect is to target speech as such rather than foreign-adversary control.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s point that naming a specific platform and risking an effective shutdown imposes substantial, non-fortuitous speech harm is the hardest issue, and Moody v. NetChoice reinforces that platforms’ operational choices can be expressive. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the Act’s trigger is foreign-adversary “control” and its remedy is divest-or-disable—structural, ownership-based regulation aimed at national-security and data-security risks, not content or viewpoint suppression—so Arcara’s conduct/expression distinction still substantially frames the inquiry, with O’Brien/Ward at most. On this emergency record, petitioners have not made the required clear showing that Congress’s rationale is pretextual or that the chosen divestiture mechanism is likely unconstitutional, and the institutional/equitable costs of enjoining Congress’s timetable in a foreign-affairs setting counsel restraint. I would deny emergency relief while leaving open that the merits briefing must confront Sotomayor’s practical-burden concerns and Moody’s implications in a fuller record.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to emphasize that naming a single platform and conditioning continued distribution on divestiture predictably burdens a major speech forum, and that burden is neither trivial nor speculative. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice note, the Act’s text makes foreign-adversary “control” the trigger and divest-or-disable the remedy; under Arcara that is regulation of ownership/control conduct with downstream expressive effects, not a facial regulation of speech, viewpoint, or editorial judgment as such. Moody v. NetChoice sharpens the inquiry by confirming platforms can engage in protected expression, yet it does not recharacterize a control-based structural condition—aimed at national-security and data-security risks—as content-based censorship; at most it points to O’Brien/Ward-style scrutiny on a full record. Given the emergency posture, Sotomayor’s irreparable-harm showing does not overcome petitioners’ failure to make the requisite clear showing of likely success, especially where the statute offers divestiture rather than compelled suppression of any particular speech.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to emphasize the practical consequence that a named-platform divest-or-disable regime can functionally eliminate a major speech forum and thus inflict irreparable harm on millions of speakers, and Moody v. NetChoice confirms that platform design/distribution can be expressive. But on this emergency posture, I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan that Arcara’s core distinction still matters: the Act’s statutory trigger is foreign-adversary “control” and the remedy is structural divestiture as a condition of U.S. distribution/hosting, not a content- or viewpoint-based restriction, making O’Brien/Ward the more plausible framework rather than treating it as speech suppression per se. Even under intermediate scrutiny, petitioners have not made the “clear showing” required for extraordinary relief that Congress’s national-security/data-security rationale is pretextual or that less speech-burdensome alternatives are so obviously effective that this tailored divestiture option is likely unconstitutional. Given the foreign-affairs/national-security context and the limited record, the equities do not justify judicially resetting Congress’s timetable absent a stronger merits showing.

John Roberts.reasoning: At this emergency stage, petitioners have not shown a clear likelihood of success on the merits or that the equities justify enjoining Congress’s chosen national-security timetable, given the Act’s focus on foreign-adversary control and data-security risks rather than suppression of speech. Under Arcara v. Cloud Books, Inc., 478 U.S. 697 (1986), a law aimed at non-expressive conduct does not trigger heightened First Amendment scrutiny merely because it incidentally burdens expressive activity, and the divestiture mechanism here is plausibly of that kind. Even assuming First Amendment scrutiny applies, a narrow, structural remedy—divestiture as an alternative to distribution restrictions—looks more like a content-neutral regulation than the content- or viewpoint-based discrimination condemned in Police Dept. of Chicago v. Mosley, 408 U.S. 92 (1972). Petitioners’ Bill of Attainder theory under Art. I, § 9, cl. 3 is not sufficiently clear on this record to justify extraordinary relief, where Congress has articulated regulatory, prospective national-security objectives rather than punishment.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Act regulates ownership and control of a communications platform by a foreign adversary, not the content of speech, and the First Amendment does not disable Congress from addressing non-expressive conduct that creates national-security risks. Under Arcara v. Cloud Books, Inc., 478 U.S. 697 (1986), incidental effects on expression do not trigger heightened scrutiny where the law targets non-expressive conduct; and nothing in the Act’s text discriminates by viewpoint as in Police Dept. of Chicago v. Mosley, 408 U.S. 92 (1972). Nor does the measure amount to a bill of attainder under U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3 because, applying Nixon v. Administrator of General Services, 433 U.S. 425 (1977), divestiture to eliminate foreign-adversary control is reasonably understood as regulatory, not historical legislative punishment. Given Congress’s chosen timetable and the public interest in mitigating asserted foreign-control risks, an emergency injunction should be denied.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Act regulates foreign-adversary control and attendant national-security/data-security risks rather than suppressing protected expression, and under Arcara v. Cloud Books, Inc., 478 U.S. 697, 706-07 (1986), a law aimed at non-expressive conduct that only incidentally burdens speech does not trigger the sort of heightened First Amendment scrutiny appropriate for direct speech regulations. Even assuming some First Amendment burden, the divestiture mechanism functions like a content- and viewpoint-neutral regulation of nonspeech conduct and would be evaluated under O’Brien-type intermediate scrutiny, which Congress can satisfy given the compelling and practical national-security consequences of foreign-adversary control. The bill-of-attainder argument is weak because the Act’s consequence is regulatory and conditional—divestiture to eliminate a foreign-control risk—rather than punitive in the constitutional sense under Art. I, § 9, cl. 3. On the emergency posture, petitioners have not met the demanding standard for an injunction pending review where Congress has set a national-security timetable and delay would undermine the public interest in promptly mitigating the identified risk.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Act compels divestiture on pain of an effective nationwide distribution/operation ban of a major communications platform, and that practical effect substantially burdens the First Amendment interests of millions of U.S. speakers and listeners, triggering meaningful scrutiny rather than Arcara-style deference to regulations with only incidental effects on expression. Unlike Arcara v. Cloud Books, Inc., 478 U.S. 697 (1986), this statute identifies a specific speech forum by name and threatens to shut it down, raising serious concerns under content-neutral but speech-burdening frameworks (O’Brien/Ward) and the Court’s recognition in Moody v. NetChoice, LLC, 144 S. Ct. 2383 (2024), that platform design and distribution decisions can implicate expressive activity. On the emergency posture, the irreparable harm to ongoing speech and associational activity during the pendency of review outweighs the government’s interest in enforcing a fixed timetable, especially where Congress chose a blunt instrument rather than narrower, less speech-restrictive data-security measures. The bill-of-attainder concern under U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3 further counsels caution where Congress singles out a named entity for severe legal consequences without an adjudicative process.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Act’s trigger is foreign-adversary control and the national-security risks Congress identified, not the suppression of particular messages, and under Arcara v. Cloud Books, Inc., 478 U.S. 697 (1986), a regulation aimed at non-expressive conduct does not become a First Amendment violation merely because it incidentally burdens expressive activity. Even accepting that TikTok’s curation and hosting involve protected expression (see Moody v. NetChoice, LLC, 144 S. Ct. 2383 (2024)), the divestiture mechanism operates as a structural ownership remedy that is content- and viewpoint-neutral and is most naturally evaluated under O’Brien-type intermediate scrutiny, which it likely satisfies given the compelling foreign-affairs and data-security interests Congress invoked. The bill-of-attainder argument is weakened by the statute’s forward-looking, regulatory design (divest-or-disable) tied to objective control criteria rather than punishment for past conduct, and the emergency injunction factors cut against relief where Congress set a specific timetable and the public-interest/national-security stakes are substantial. On this record, I would deny an emergency injunction pending review and vote to uphold the Act.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: On the Act’s face, Congress regulates foreign-adversary control of a communications platform and conditions continued U.S. distribution on divestiture, a form of regulation aimed at nonexpressive ownership/control rather than the content of any user’s speech. Under Arcara v. Cloud Books, a law that neither targets expressive conduct nor has the inevitable effect of singling out speech activity does not trigger heightened First Amendment scrutiny, and any incidental burden would be evaluated at most under O’Brien/Ward-type intermediate scrutiny, where national security and data-protection interests are weighty and the divestiture mechanism is a tailored means to address control. The bill-of-attainder argument is difficult to square with the Act’s prospective, regulatory structure—conditioning market access on ownership attributes—rather than imposing a traditional punitive sanction forbidden by Art. I, § 9, cl. 3. Given the equities and Congress’s chosen timetable, petitioners have not shown the clear likelihood of success and irreparable injury necessary for an emergency injunction pending review.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: An emergency injunction should be denied because the Act is best understood as a national-security and foreign-adversary control measure regulating ownership/control and data-security risks, not a law aimed at suppressing speech, and under Arcara v. Cloud Books it does not target “conduct with a significant expressive element” or have the “inevitable effect” of singling out expressive activity for burden. Even assuming some First Amendment scrutiny applies, the divestiture requirement resembles regulation of nonexpressive conduct with only incidental effects on expression and is likely workable under intermediate-scrutiny frameworks (O’Brien/Ward) given Congress’s compelling foreign-affairs and national-security interests and the Act’s tailored remedy of divestiture rather than direct content regulation. The petitioners also have not shown a clear likelihood of success on their bill-of-attainder theory under U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3 because the statute operates as a prospective regulatory condition on distribution/hosting tied to foreign-adversary control rather than a punitive adjudication of guilt. On the equitable factors, delaying the statutory timetable would significantly disrupt Congress’s chosen national-security response, and the Court should proceed with restraint and deference in this sensitive area while maintaining institutional stability.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Act’s text regulates foreign-adversary “control” of a covered application and conditions continued U.S. distribution/hosting on divestiture, which is most naturally read as targeting nonexpressive ownership and data-security risk rather than suppressing speech. Under Arcara v. Cloud Books, Inc., 478 U.S. 697, 706-07 (1986), a law directed at nonexpressive conduct does not trigger heightened First Amendment scrutiny merely because it incidentally burdens expressive activity, and this statute’s national-security rationale does not single out speech as such. Even assuming First Amendment scrutiny applies, the divestiture mechanism is plausibly content- and viewpoint-neutral and can be evaluated under an O’Brien/Ward-style intermediate scrutiny framework, where Congress’s asserted foreign-adversary national-security interest is compelling and the means are not facially aimed at speech. On the emergency posture, petitioners have not made the requisite strong showing of likely success on the merits to justify an injunction that would effectively rewrite Congress’s chosen timetable in Pub. L. 118-50.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: At the emergency-injunction stage, TikTok has not made the requisite strong showing of likelihood of success on the merits or that the balance of equities and the public interest favor overriding Congress’s national-security timetable in the Protecting Americans From Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act. Under Arcara v. Cloud Books, the Act is best characterized as regulating non-expressive conduct—foreign-adversary control and associated data-security risks—rather than targeting speech, because it does not on its face draw distinctions aimed at suppressing expression or inevitably single out expressive activity as such. Even assuming First Amendment scrutiny applies, the divestiture mechanism can be evaluated under an O’Brien-type framework as an incidental burden on speech in service of a substantial interest unrelated to suppression, and the requested injunction would risk material practical consequences in an area where courts traditionally proceed with caution. The bill-of-attainder framing is weakened by the Act’s forward-looking, regulatory structure and its use of a conditional divestiture regime rather than a legislative determination of guilt and punishment under U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3.
